html:
A cemetery of stone burial towers on the shore of Lake Umayo near Puno, in the Peruvian highlands near Lake Titicaca. The towers, called chullpas, were built for the elite of the Qulla people, probably speakers of the Puquina language, in the centuries before and during their conquest by the Inca in the 15th century. They are also described as the tombs of the Aymara elite.

Each tower held a whole family group, most likely of noble rank. The bodies were laid in a curled position and not mummified on purpose, but the closed, dry towers kept them for centuries. The only opening of each tower faces east, where the sun was believed to be reborn each day. Burial above ground in such towers goes back across the southern Andes at least to the time of Tiwanaku (about 500 to 950). Some of the older towers at Sillustani were later refaced with the fitted stone blocks typical of the Inca, and some have animals carved on them.

Sillustani is considered the best preserved of the many chullpa sites on the high plain. Several towers were never finished, and a ramp still leans against one of them, showing how the builders hauled stones up the walls. Grave robbers blew many of the towers open with dynamite. Some have been restored, including in a project of 2005.
